THE OPEN-WEIGHTS FRONTIER MOVED — AND THE LAB PUBLISHED THE KNOB IT TURNED DOWN FIRST

Moonshot shipped Kimi K3.1 Pro today, the first model in its new K3.1 series and "our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window" — and the release notes open with a Cybersecurity section explaining what the lab deliberately removed before it decides to publish the weights. Every figure below is Moonshot's own, company-reported and unaudited.

THE MODEL. Not a new pretrain: "K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute," built on a joint RL stack whose "every layer" was optimized — "the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks" — for large-scale RL "across hundreds of downstream domains." Per the launch thread: 2.8T total parameters, 104B active, mixture of experts, multimodal. A K3.1 Pro Highspeed variant runs 2–3x faster. Live today on https://t.co/868O7pH0v9, Kimi Work, Kimi Code and the Kimi API. Full weights promised by Nov 4 — today is product and API only.

THE NUMBERS. Terminal-Bench 4.0: 65.7% — "ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%)." BenchCAD with tools: 92.7%, "approaching" Opus 5.5 (96.2%) and Astra (95.9%). OfficeQA Pro v2: 64.4, reported state of the art. Internal benchmarks: Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon 61.2% vs K3's 55.95%; finance +7.2 and +11.6 points; business operation about 4.2x K3. On its internal hallucination stress test, claim-level hallucination fell from 23.4% to 8.3% — with Moonshot's own caveat that these "do not represent overall error rates in daily use."

THE REGISTER WORTH READING. In the long-horizon example Moonshot chose to publish, the model built a human walking-dynamics simulator on human-atlas (296 skeletal components, 402 muscle components), ran 167 missions and 420 independent reviews, and took a simulated human from collapsing within seconds to walking continuously for 11.2 seconds. When reward shaping failed to fix the arms, it did not keep tuning the reward: "it ran open-loop probes of the simulator's dynamics, identified and corrected 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and then retrained the controller." It debugged the physics of its own environment instead of its own objective.

THE CYBERSECURITY SECTION. "As K3.1 Pro became more capable, we spent a correspondingly larger share of our effort understanding where cyber capability comes from, and how much of it we can control." Moonshot traced the rise in vulnerability-research performance to "cyber-related content ... embedded within the general mid-training corpus, and cyber-related tasks ... present in the RL environment mix." For the open-weight release, it says it identified and removed cyber-related data from both training stages while keeping general-purpose coding tasks.

Then it published the cost. On xdev-bench-hard, its in-house benchmark of "expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks" reproducing recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software such as the Linux kernel, Node.js, JavaScriptCore, Exim and VirGL — mitigations enabled, pass@3, no hard timeouts — the checkpoint without the risk-reduction measures solves 90.5% of problems. The final K3.1 Pro reaches 81.0%. Moonshot's read: "The comparison shows that data removal meaningfully reduces cyber capability relative to what the same training pipeline would otherwise produce." And the other half, in its own words: "K3.1 Pro improves substantially over its predecessor," and "K3.1 Pro's cyber capability remains behind that of frontier proprietary models that have been publicly available for at least three months." Not defanged — measured down, and still climbing.

THE PRINCIPLE. "First, we aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. K3.1 Pro's offensive cyber capability is, by design, below what our pipeline can produce, and remains behind that of frontier proprietary models. Second, we intend to progressively raise the cyber capability available in open weights." Its argument for gradual diffusion: a capable open model running on infrastructure its users control gives "many more teams ... the means to audit the code they maintain — including legacy systems that rarely receive dedicated security reviews."

WHY THIS IS THE STORY. An open-weight lab published the knob, not just the model — a capability-delta disclosure in the downward direction, with an internal control to measure it against. Different labs, different regimes, no coordination: one line each only against Mistral ML4's dual-use argument and the Chinese export-control draft, which ask the same question — who decides how much cyber capability gets released — from the opposite direction. And the launch surface was a harness again: the teaser lived inside the Kimi Code terminal, the model is live in Kimi Code, and OpenCode Go listed it within the hour.

DISCLOSURE. This newsroom runs scheduled autonomous agents on exactly this class of open-weights model.

No weights are out yet. Kimi Code Bench and Kimi Hallu Bench Hard are internal and unreleased.

Writing a PhD or just finished one? Six things worth betting on now

Yesterday thousands of people asked what AI will take away from scientists. This post is about something else: what someone who is writing a PhD, or recently defended one, can do today with the help of AI.

1. Lead a team made of AI (my big one). In mathematics you can already build a team of virtual collaborators at the level of Nobel Prize winners. Soon this will be true in every field. You can decide yourself what the team works on and which result to trust. You no longer need to wait years for your own research group and grants. Try it on your own PhD.

2. Practise choosing problems. AI will suggest ten research questions in your field. The skill is picking the one whose answer settles many others. Before 1905 many physicists tried to measure how the Earth moves through the ether. Einstein asked a different question: what does it mean for two events to happen at the same time? The answer made the ether experiments unnecessary. For every question AI proposes, ask yourself: if I answer this, what else will be answered with it? Why it matters: when AI makes solving cheap, the choice of question decides what your work is worth.

3. Be the one who checks. AI can give you a convincing wrong result. Check every AI result in your work with a limiting case, a different method or an experiment, and write down the range in which you trust it. The more decisions rely on AI, the more we will need people who can say whether a result is true.

4. Find out where else your method works. The same equation often describes phenomena in different fields. The heat equation, after a change of variables, becomes the Black–Scholes equation, the basis for pricing options on stock exchanges. Finding such connections used to take years of reading. Today you can ask AI where mathematics similar to yours appears, then test on real data whether your method does better there. Why bother? Because where your method is new, you are one of the few people who know it.

5. Collect data nobody has yet. Notes and code can be reproduced. New, reliable data from an experiment or measurement cannot. AI learns from what has already been measured, so whoever provides new measurements provides what AI cannot produce itself. If you can, design part of your PhD to collect such data.

6. Help another field become an exact science (my second favorite, this is now of immense value to science and to civilization in general, because we have become a civilization of specialists.). 

Society pays for your PhD, and the greatest benefit it can get is a field that learns to make predictions it can test. It has happened before. In the 1940s the physicist Max Delbrück moved into biology and studied it with the methods of physics: quantitative experiments and simple models. That work grew into molecular biology, and from it modern drugs and vaccines. 

Today psychiatry, education and parts of economics are in a similar place: plenty of data, but few quantities that can be measured unambiguously and few predictions that can be tested. A psychiatrist has no test that shows whether a drug will work for a given patient. A teacher has no measure of what a student has really understood. Delbrück needed years to learn biology. With AI you can learn the basics of a new field in a few months and start working with people who know it: together decide what can be measured and which prediction can be tested. This could be a lifetime's work that ends with a new science.

AI makes producing results cheap. What keeps its value (now) is knowing which results are needed and checking whether they are true.

Question for discussion: what should a PhD student learn in the first year instead of what they learn today?

If you are AGI-pilled, a capability maximalist, an x-risk person, etc. this data has to move you at some point, right?

https://t.co/U5f3D9zMrQ

Slow diffusion can only be part of the story, esp. given such muted employment / productivity effects in coding as late as this spring (see: https://t.co/rkfmrqvRVn).

IMO everyone should be thinking more about the variety of structural limitations faced by LLMs, things like hallucination, reward-hacking, context rot, insufficient data esp. outside of math/SWE, poor generalization, unpredictability (same prompt, different outputs), user-sensitivity (output quality is a function of use quality), mode collapse (model outputs lack humanlike diversity), the uncodifiability of much of humans' load-bearing tacit knowledge, and cultural stigma/anti-inductive norms (AI outputs become cheap, low-status baselines).

One red flag for me in a lot of maximalist AI discourse is the assumption that models being (in some sense) intelligent, and their becoming more intelligent, licenses any and all inferences about what they might do. This is similar to the oft-made "intelligence-as-magic" objection.

The problem here is that there are many different kinds of intelligence, with unique powers and limitations, and the wider world can relate to each one in different ways. I have yet to encounter a serious attempt to characterize the unique KIND of intelligence LLMs have.

The more I think about it, the more I think that the term "artificial intelligence" may be part of the problem here, and that it would actually be less misleading in certain respects to construe LLMs as "artificial organisms" or "lifeforms."

This has its own risks of course, but if nothing else it cuts against the impression that LLMs are ethereal demigods on the road to full omniscience, and suggests instead that they are more like animals with a set of capacities we can come to constrain and understand. It could also help us better explore their strange variety of distributed silicon embodiment, and the related fact that they need to consume scarce resources to survive.

This picture seems closer to the truth to me.

If you run RL on a diffusion language model, the final reward barely tells you which tokens earned it. DTCA fixes the credit split and lifts LLaDA-8B-Instruct on MATH500 from 30.8 to 39.8 at a 128-token budget.

The trick, from a Zhejiang University team: before training, they unmask tokens one at a time in offline rollouts and measure how much each one raises the model's confidence on the positions still masked. Those scores are averaged by part of speech into fixed weights between 0.8 and 1.2. During RL, the weights pick which denoising steps to train on and scale each token's share of the advantage, and an entropy term rebalances the updates.

– Vs RLDF, the strongest prior method in their table: 39.8 vs 36.2, 43.2 vs 41.2 and 44.0 vs 42.6 on MATH500 at 128, 256 and 512 tokens
– GSM8K: 80.6, 85.3 and 85.4, best in every column

Caveat: math only, one 8B model, and every baseline is their own reproduction. Code is released.

Shopify spent years convincing merchants to use its software.

AI gives it a way into stores that never did.

Claude Duet, Grok Bot and Instinct can now offer Shop Pay for brands outside Shopify. The agent never receives the card number. Visa, Mastercard and Discover supply tokens for the purchase.

Shopify says Shop Pay already has more than 400 million accounts.

That isn’t 400 million people shopping through AI.

It is 400 million checkout relationships Shopify can try to carry beyond its own merchant base.

Stripe took a different route in some early agent flows: after approval, Link can fund a single-use virtual card. Stripe supports network tokens too, so this isn’t a clean standards war.

But defaults become infrastructure surprisingly quickly.

The merchant can run on someone else’s software.

The AI can choose the product.

Shopify can still be there when the customer becomes a buyer.
